newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK M2 SLOWS BUT C.BANK UNLIKELY TO EASE POLICY.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK M2 SLOWS BUT C.BANK UNLIKELY TO EASE POLICY.

text.p: The Slovak central bank (NBS) is unlikely to ease its tight monetary policy in the first half of 1997 despite a consistent slow-down in growth of the key money supply aggregate, M2, analysts said on Monday.

The NBS said on Monday M2, its main yardstick for assessing monetary development, grew 12.8 percent year-on-year in March 1997, after a 13.9 percent increase in February. This compares with a 24.1 percent increase in March 1996.
But analysts said that new factors on the horizon preclude the central bank from easing its tight monetary policy in the near-term.

"There are some new factors that should be taken into account regarding M2 and monetary policy such as the new import deposit measure," Sylvia Majlingova, Liquidity Department Director at CSOB Bank, told Reuters.

"Even though we think that the central bank should have some room to ease its strict policy -- through lower minimun reserves requirement -- this is not likely to happen in the first half of the year," she added.
The NBS full year target for M2 growth is 10.7 percent.
Majlingova was referring to a new measure requiring importers of selected consumer goods to deposit 20 percent of the value of imports on an interest-free account for six months.

"Much would depend on where these funds (import deposits) will end up. If they are held in the NBS and do not enter the banking sector, the measure will drain liquidity and further slow M2 growth," Majlingova said.

"(And) if the collected money -- mainly from short-term time deposits of small importers -- were held out of the banking sector and push M2 further down, the full year target will become attainable," she added.
NBS Governor Vladimir Masar said last week that the bank could reconsider its monetary policy if the funds collected from import deposits were held on its account.
The government and central bank have agreed that the money would be channelled to the NBS through state-run Konsolidacna Banka. But the NBS and cabinet have yet to agree on the use of the funds.
Anna Glasova, Head of the Dealing at Slovenska Sporitelna said she also saw a possible loosening of monetary polcy linked to the import deposits.
"We think that the NBS will wait with reconsidering its policy until the end of the first half of the year when the use of the funds from import deposits will be clear," she said.
Masar said the NBS expected the overall amount of import deposits would not exceed 10 billion crowns by the end of June.
